questions.prompt: What does Anthropic warn can happen when agents run on their own?

options.text: Costs rise and errors can compound, so it recommends testing in sandboxes
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic names higher costs and the potential for compounding errors.

options.text: The agents always refuse to use tools, so they cannot do any useful work
options.explanation: Anthropic does not say this. It says agents can use tools and recover from errors.

options.text: Agents become cheaper with each loop, so cost is never a problem for any team
options.explanation: Anthropic says the opposite: autonomy means higher costs.

questions.prompt: When does OpenAI's orchestration guide say to add a specialist agent?

options.text: For every step of the job, so that each step can have its own agent from the start
options.explanation: The guide warns against splitting too early.

options.text: When it materially improves isolation, prompt clarity, or trace legibility for the job
options.explanation: Right. The guide lists capability isolation, policy isolation, prompt clarity and trace legibility.

options.text: Never, because the guide says every agent system must always have exactly one agent
options.explanation: The guide says to start with one agent, and to add specialists when they help.

questions.prompt: How long does Google keep an inactive managed-agent environment?

options.text: For ever, as long as the account stays open and paid up
options.explanation: Google says inactive environments are deleted.

options.text: For 24 hours, and after that a new one is made for you
options.explanation: The agents page gives 7 days of inactivity, not 24 hours.

options.text: It deletes them permanently after 7 days of inactivity
options.explanation: Right. Google's page says environments are permanently deleted after 7 days of inactivity.
